description: Aims, hypotheses and sampling. Qualitative vs quantitative, primary vs secondary and official statistics.
content_html:
Planning Research: Aims, Hypotheses and Pilot Studies

Before collecting a single piece of data, sociologists must make a series of decisions about what they want to find out and how. Research aims define the purpose of a study — for example, “to investigate factors affecting GCSE attainment among students from different socioeconomic backgrounds.” From the aim, the researcher usually develops a hypothesis — a precise, testable prediction, such as “students eligible for free school meals will achieve lower GCSE grades than those who are not.” The hypothesis gives the research direction and allows the findings to be evaluated.

A pilot study is a small-scale test of the research instrument before the main study begins. Imagine a sociologist designing a questionnaire to study attitudes to arranged marriage among young adults in the East Midlands. Running the questionnaire with ten participants first might reveal that a key question is ambiguous, that the response options are too few, or that the time taken is longer than expected. Pilot studies save time and resources by identifying flaws before they contaminate the main data.

Key Fact

The research design process follows a sequence: aim (what do you want to find out?) → hypothesis (what do you predict?) → method choice (how will you gather data?) → sampling (who will you study?) → pilot study (test and refine) → main data collection → analysis.

Sampling: Who to Study?

Sociologists rarely study entire populations. Instead, they select a sample from a sampling frame (a list of the population). The goal is usually a representative sample — one that accurately reflects the characteristics of the wider population, so that findings can be generalised beyond the sample itself.

There are five main sampling methods you need to know:

  • Random sample — every member of the sampling frame has an equal chance of selection. This minimises bias but requires a complete list of the population.
  • Systematic sample — every nth person from the list is selected (e.g. every tenth name). Practical but may introduce bias if the list has a pattern at every nth interval.
  • Stratified sample — the population is divided into groups (strata) by relevant characteristics (e.g. social class, gender) and a proportional number is selected from each stratum. This ensures the sample mirrors the structure of the population.
  • Quota sample — the researcher sets quotas for particular groups (e.g. 50 working-class women, 50 middle-class women) and then selects participants non-randomly until quotas are filled. Quick and inexpensive but non-random, so technically not fully representative.
  • Snowball sample — initial participants recruit others from their networks. Useful for hidden or hard-to-reach populations (e.g. studying drug use, gang membership), but the sample is unlikely to be representative of a wider population.

A sociologist wants to investigate attitudes to higher education among Year 11 students at a comprehensive school in South Yorkshire. The school has 200 Year 11 students. Using a stratified sample, the researcher identifies key strata (e.g. gender, eligibility for free school meals, ethnicity) and selects a proportional number from each group. This increases representativeness — if 30% of students are eligible for free school meals, approximately 30% of the sample will be too, ensuring the findings reflect the full diversity of the year group. A snowball sample would be inappropriate here because students are not a hard-to-reach population and the resulting sample would be biased towards social networks.

Types of Data: Quantitative and Qualitative

Quantitative data takes numerical form — percentages, rates, frequencies, scores. It allows comparisons across large samples, can be analysed statistically, and is associated with approaches that aim for objectivity and replicability. A national survey of 10,000 households can identify patterns and trends in family forms, income or crime rates with a precision no qualitative study can match.

Qualitative data takes verbal form — the words, accounts, feelings and interpretations of research participants. It provides depth and texture, exploring the meanings behind behaviour. An in-depth interview with a family discussing domestic division of labour may reveal nuances about negotiation, resentment and expectation that a tick-box questionnaire would miss entirely.

The choice between quantitative and qualitative approaches often reflects the sociologist’s theoretical perspective. Positivists (associated with functionalism and some Marxist approaches) prefer quantitative data, arguing sociology should emulate natural science. Interpretivists (associated with interactionism) prefer qualitative data, arguing that understanding social behaviour requires grasping the subjective meanings of the participants. In practice, many researchers use mixed methods — combining both types to exploit their complementary strengths.

Primary and Secondary Data; Official Statistics

Primary data is original data collected directly by the researcher. Secondary data is data already gathered by someone else that the researcher re-uses — government statistics, newspaper archives, historical records, published studies.

A very common error is to treat official statistics — figures produced by government departments such as ONS or the Home Office — as straightforward facts. Sociologists are trained to evaluate them critically. Official statistics have strengths: they are large-scale, nationally consistent, free to use, and allow trends to be tracked over time. However, they have important limitations. Crime statistics, for example, only count crimes that are reported to and recorded by the police; the “dark figure” of unreported and unrecorded crime means official figures systematically underestimate the true level of offending. Different perspectives also interpret the same statistics differently: a functionalist might see declining crime rates as evidence of effective social control; a Marxist might argue that statistics reflect selective policing of working-class communities; an interactionist might argue the statistics tell us more about police labelling practices than about actual behaviour. Always evaluate, never just cite.

Key Fact

The five sampling methods are: random, systematic, stratified, quota and snowball. Stratified sampling is best when the researcher wants the sample to mirror the social structure of the population. Snowball sampling is best for hard-to-reach populations where a sampling frame does not exist.
exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Describe about data types or sampling, avoid listing without explaining. A common exam error is to write “quantitative data is numerical and qualitative data is words” and stop there — that is two identifications, not two descriptions. For 4 marks you need to develop each point: explain what makes numerical data useful for sociological research (large-scale, statistically testable, comparable across groups) and what makes qualitative data useful (depth, explores meanings, reveals what statistics miss). Linking to a named method or theoretical perspective (e.g. “positivists prefer quantitative data because…”) lifts the answer further. On the 12-mark Discuss, evaluation of official statistics must be in context — not just “statistics can be wrong” but explaining exactly why the specific statistics are problematic for the research question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Research design follows a sequence: aim → hypothesis → method → sampling → pilot study → data collection → analysis. Pilot studies test and refine instruments before the main study.
  • Five sampling methods: random (equal chance), systematic (every nth), stratified (proportional by group), quota (non-random quotas) and snowball (for hard-to-reach populations). The aim is a representative sample that allows findings to be generalised.
  • Quantitative data (numbers) suits large-scale pattern-finding; qualitative data (words) suits in-depth meaning. Official statistics are secondary data with both strengths (scale, consistency) and weaknesses (under-reporting, political production) that sociologists must always evaluate critically.

practice_questions.text:
Which sampling method involves selecting every tenth person from a list of the population?
A) Random sample
B) Quota sample
C) Systematic sample
D) Snowball sample
Define the term 'hypothesis' as used in sociological research.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for indicating a hypothesis is a prediction or statement to be tested; 1 mark for indicating it predicts a relationship between variables and can be supported or refuted by evidence. Example: 'A hypothesis is a specific, testable prediction about a relationship between two or more variables, stated before data collection and either supported or refuted by the findings.'

practice_questions.text: Identify one advantage of using a pilot study and describe how it would improve the quality of a sociological investigation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying an advantage (e.g. identifies flaws in questions, reveals ambiguity, indicates how long the study will take, tests whether the sampling method is practical). Up to 2 marks for a developed description. Example: identifying that a pilot study identifies ambiguous questions (1 mark) and explaining that if a question is unclear to respondents, different participants will interpret it differently, reducing the validity and reliability of the data; revising the question after the pilot ensures all participants understand it in the same way (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between quantitative and qualitative data, and explain why sociologists might choose one over the other.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for describing the difference: quantitative data is numerical (percentages, rates, counts) and allows statistical analysis and large-scale comparison; qualitative data is verbal (words, accounts, meanings) and provides depth and insight into participants' experiences. Up to 2 marks for explaining a reason to choose one. Example: a sociologist studying national patterns of divorce might choose quantitative data (ONS statistics) because it allows trends over time to be identified across the whole population; a sociologist studying the experience of family breakdown for individual children might choose qualitative data (in-depth interviews) because the lived experience requires depth of understanding that statistics cannot provide.

practice_questions.text: Identify one limitation of using official statistics as a source of data in sociological research and describe how this affects the validity of conclusions drawn from them.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying a limitation of official statistics (e.g. under-reporting, dark figure of crime, political production, recording inconsistencies between police forces, changing legal definitions). Up to 2 marks for developing the description. Example: identifying under-reporting (1 mark) and explaining that many crimes are never reported to the police — particularly domestic violence and sexual assault — so official crime statistics significantly undercount the true level of offending; any conclusions about crime patterns drawn from official statistics may therefore reflect reporting behaviour rather than actual crime, threatening the validity of the findings (2 marks).

practice_questions.text: "Official statistics are the most useful source of data for sociological research." How far would sociologists agree with this view?
practice_questions.type: 12 marks — Discuss How Far Sociologists Would Agree
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Arguments in favour include: official statistics cover the entire population, are free to access, allow long-term trend analysis, and carry the authority of consistent national collection (e.g. ONS, Crime Survey for England and Wales). Arguments against include: official statistics are produced by governments and may reflect political priorities; crime statistics are limited by the dark figure of unreported and unrecorded crime; different sociological perspectives interpret the same statistics differently (functionalist, Marxist and interactionist readings of crime data diverge significantly); qualitative data may offer insight that statistics obscure. The answer cites at least two sociological perspectives or contexts (e.g. crime vs family research), evaluates specific strengths and weaknesses in context, and reaches a clear supported judgement. Sustained sociological vocabulary.

Secure: Both strengths and limitations addressed. At least one sociological perspective cited. A judgement reached.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or descriptive. Some evaluation but undeveloped. Conclusion present but not substantiated.

Emerging: Basic points about what statistics are. Little evaluation. No clear judgement.
